Metaphysics. The philosophical inquiry into the fundamental nature of reality: what exists, what is the relationship between mind and matter, whether change and time are real, and whether there are universal substances or forms underlying appearances. The name derives from Aristotle's works arranged after the physics, but the questions predate him. The pre-Socratics obsessed over being and non-being, permanence and change. Metaphysics remains the most ambitious and controversial branch of philosophy because it claims knowledge about what lies beyond the physical, yet its objects—being, substance, causation—are inherently difficult to define and verify.

Parmenides posed the founding problem. If something changes, does it become something other than itself, violating the law of non-contradiction? His radical conclusion was that change is illusion and true being is eternal and unchanging. This haunted all subsequent metaphysics. Aristotle named the field and gave it structure. Metaphysics asks what is substance—the independent thing that exists—what is form, the organizing principle, what is actuality, the realized being, and what is causation through the four causes: material, efficient, formal, and final.

The mind-body problem is metaphysics' most urgent modern puzzle. If the physical world is all that exists, how do consciousness and subjective experience arise? Is the mind physical, immaterial, or a fundamental feature of reality? Substance dualism, associated with Descartes, posits two substances—mind and matter—solving the problem by denying physicalism, but it generates the interaction problem: how do immaterial thoughts cause physical actions?

Materialism, or physicalism, argues that only physical substances and properties exist; mental phenomena are either identical to brain states or reduced to them. This avoids dualism's problems but struggles to explain consciousness. Idealism flips the equation: reality consists fundamentally of mind, ideas, or consciousness; the physical world is mind-dependent. This preserves the uniqueness of consciousness but seems counterintuitive about external objects.

Metaphysicians debate whether universals—properties, kinds, numbers—exist independent of the physical world or are merely conventional patterns imposed by minds. This is the problem of universals, dating to Plato and Aristotle. Modern physics has unsettled metaphysics profoundly. Simultaneity is relative; particles exist in superposition until measured; spacetime is curved. The metaphysical interpretation of physics remains contested.

Metaphysics connects to Aristotle, who named the field and systematized its central questions. Parmenides posed the founding crisis about change and being. The pre-Socratics were the first metaphysicians, debating the nature of ultimate reality. Descartes revived substance dualism in the modern era and sharpened the mind-body problem. Kant argued that space and time are structures of the mind, not properties of things-in-themselves. Metaphysics is the heart of philosophy; all other branches depend on metaphysical assumptions. And consciousness is the central phenomenon metaphysics struggles to explain.
